Proteas' 2015 World Cup Campaign

By: Etienne Naude | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We spend some time with the Proteas ahead of their 2015 Cricket World Cup campaign, and see how they’re going to take the #ProteaFire spirit with them Down Under.

Summary:
The Proteas have provided some of South African sport’s most iconic and celebrated moments. We will briefly recap some of the highlights from the last 6 Cricket World Cups. We will interview some current players, including AB de Villiers, about the spirit and culture of the ultimate “nice guy” team, and get them to share their hopes and expectations for the 2015 World Cup, and what they think their chances are of lifting cricket’s most coveted trophy for the first time.

Further information:
The Proteas are not only cricketers. They see themselves as ambassadors for South Africa. When they play cricket, they are not only playing for themselves, but for a whole nation of supporters. Cricket South Africa’s launch of the #ProteaFire campaign is about getting the public to better identify with the players and understand the values that the team lives by – humility, resilience, courage, adaptability, unity and respect. It is the Proteas’ mission to inspire South Africans through their actions on and off the field. It is this culture that we will explore and focus the insert around.
We will also speak to former players or captains, to reflect on how the game has changed, reminisce about their fondest memories from previous World Cups, and share their thoughts on the current Proteas squad – both as a team of cricketers, and South African ambassadors.

Press Release:


Protea Fire
On Sunday the Proteas will play their first game of the 2015 Cricket World Cup. Carte Blanche sat down with Captain AB de Villiers and his team, just before they departed for Australia and New Zealand, to hear one question answered: will they be bringing home the coveted cup?


Script:


PROTEAS INSERT FULL SCRIPT

BONGANI:
It was just last month when AB de Villiers made history here at the Wanderers stadium by scoring the fastest ever 50 and century in One-Day Internationals, smashing his way into the cricket hall of fame.

BONGANI VO
That performance cemented his position as the top one-day batsman in the world, and bodes well for South Africa’s confidence going into the World Cup.

BONGANI:
As an individual player you’re probably in the best form of your life. You’re now being rated by the likes of Viv Richards and Adam Gilchrist as the most exciting player. That must be a personal boost on some level.

AB DE VILLIERS:
Ja it feels good. I’ve always been the kind of guy to keep my feet on the ground. I grew up in that way. My brothers would never allow me to get big-headed. I take it in my stride and I try not to get too excited about it. I have had a couple of good years. But there are more important things than just my own performance. I want to be a good captain. I want to win games. I want to be a good influence on my teammates. Those things count a lot more than just scoring runs and getting accolades from other guys.

BONGANI
It’s all about the team for you, isn’t it?

AB DE VILLIERS
100%.

BONGANI VO
AB’s knock may actually have transformed the sport, according to cricket veteran Fanie de Villiers.

FANIE DE VILLIERS
Just what happened with the knock with AB de Villiers… He evolved the game unbelievably to the next level. The perception the kids have now of the shots they can play – the guys are going to start training those. You’re going to have many more players playing the kind of knock AB played at the Wanderers, which was completely unorthodox.

BONGANI VO
South African cricket has indeed come a long way since our first World Cup appearance 23 years ago, where there was drama from the very first ball. Allan Donald’s blinding opening ball was edged to the keeper, but the umpire didn’t give the decision. That’s a perfect summary of South Africa’s World Cup fortunes – brilliance and bad luck. Despite being one of the world’s most consistently top-ranked teams, the World Cup Trophy has mysteriously eluded the Proteas. Even cricket experts like commentator and former Zimbabwean player Pommie Mbangwa aren’t entirely sure why.

BONGANI
South Africa haven’t been able to go all the way. Why is that?

POMMI MBANGWA
I don’t know. It’s a question that will be asked until it’s actually done. The one thing I’ll say is that over time it’s become a heavier and heavier burden.

FANIE DE VILLIERS
The question that I would pose is, “Were we good enough to win the World Cup in the past?” We’re probably good enough now to say if this team doesn’t do it, then we need to ask why.

BONGANI VO
We had to bring up the dreaded “C”-word with the captain.

BONGANI
The Proteas do have a reputation of not winning on big stages – the so-called “choking” label. How are you preparing for that?

AB DE VILLIERS
I thought in the first part of your question you weren’t going to say that word. But we don’t mind hearing that word. It’s definitely not a nice tag to have. It is part of our history and there’s nothing we can do about it. The only thing we can focus on is to go and win that cup now. I think that thing will disappear very quickly then.

BONGANI VO
The Proteas’ reputation as the ultimate nice guys of South African sport is well earned, as we heard from Cricket South Africa’s Marc Jury.

MARC JURY
If you look at things like the Proteas playing in pink. Those are things that they’ve thrown their weight behind. They’re just a great bunch of guys who are superb cricketers and are going out to represent their country. You know, playing in pink for the pink day, going to visit Kieran Adams in Southfields. I think they understand the responsibility they’ve got and the impact they can have on South Africans.

BONGANI VO
This home visit was part of the #ProteaFire campaign, which is about showing that the Proteas belong to all of South Africa. The players making their world cup debuts this year, like Aaron Phangiso, treasure that spirit.

AARON PHANGISO
This is my honest opinion – I feel that our team represents everyone. It doesn’t matter which race or culture. I think we’ve got it right.

AB DE VILLIERS
The team culture is probably our biggest strength. So many different and unique people in our team. We get that team to work together. That’s very powerful.

BONGANI VO
The philosophy of #ProteaFire – playing as role models with values and a purpose larger than just cricket – began with former Proteas captain Graeme Smith.

BONGANI
Tell me about the origins of #ProteaFire.

GRAEME SMITH
We’d always just seen the Protea as a flower. We found out it was the first flower to regenerate after a fire, so fire and resilience became key things in our value system. We found out that Proteus was the Greek god. Because he could see the future he had to tell the truth, so honesty and truth. And to see how that has grown from a value perspective and the respect for the different cultures and diversity we have has been incredible.

BONGANI
As ambassadors, what would you want young kids to learn from those values?

GRAEME SMITH
I think the most important thing is to have a dream. This opportunity to represent South Africa and play for the Proteas was something I wanted youngsters to still endeavor to do.

BONGANI
For kids like this – primary cricket enthusiasts – the Proteas are big role models. And it would appear the spirit of #ProteaFire is contagious.

BONGANI
What does #ProteaFire mean to you?

Vox Pop:
It means that it helps you with your cricket. Thinking that they’re behind me, it’s the fire, and then you play your heart out and do the best you can.
Vox Pop:
Everything they do is all together.
Vox Pop:
It makes me feel like I’m a Protea. One day I’ll be up on that stage hopefully. So that’s why I get fired up.
Vox Pop:
I like the way they bat and bowl.
Vox Pop:
It means everything to them. More and more kids are taking cricket. They’re very passionate. They’ve got a fire burning in their hearts to support the Proteas and the sport of cricket.
Vox Pop:
It inspires me to do my best and score runs and take wickets.

BONGANI
The players know how many children like this look up to them.

FARHAAN BERHARDIEN
Definitely. We are role models. I grew up on the Cape Flats. For me and my peers it’s quite a big thing. Being that shining light does play a big role in how we carry ourselves on and off the field.

BONGANI VO
Hopefully this year, that ProteaFire magic will produce more spectacular moments, as the cricket World Cup always has in the past. Like Jonty Rhodes’s flying run-out of Inzamam ul-Haq in 1992, or Lance Klusener blasting his way to Player of the Tournament in 1999. And then there’ve been the notorious mishaps – dropped bats and dropped catches that swung crucial games. And the rain has never been kind to the Proteas, most notoriously in 1992, in South Africa’s semi-final against England, when a convoluted method of adjusting targets in the event of a rain delay revised South Africa’s target of needing 22 runs from 13 balls to needing 22 runs from 1 ball.

POMMIE MBANGWA
Many a South African will see those pictures of Kepler Wessels and the rest of them standing there and walking out onto the field and shaking hands with the English guys. Absolutely nothing you can do. That’s probably the worst one in terms of being powerless, because it’s the rules that make it like that, and you’re gone. Thanks for coming.

BONGANI VO
But win or lose, the Proteas have always had enormous support from their fans. A major event at Melrose Arch gave their supporters a chance to show their passion for the Proteas just before they flew out to Australia. T20 Captain Faf du Plessis speaks for the whole squad about how much the fans back home inspire them.

FAF DU PLESSIS
It makes a huge difference. The Aussies, especially, when you play against them… they’re really tough fans. They really get behind their people. When you go there and you play against them, you know you’re playing against them. So the fans help you a lot with that.

BONGANI
Well I’d pay a lot of money to see you beat Australia.

FAF DU PLESSIS
I’ll pay that money as well. In the final, that’d be great.

GRAEME SMITH
When you take on Australia, once you land there, the media, the public, everyone turns against you for the 6 weeks that you’re there.

BONGANI VO
But having the world’s top 2 one-day batsmen and the world’s top fast bowler in our squad surely gives the fans higher hopes than ever before.

POMMIE MBANGWA
AB de Villiers, Hashim Amla and Dale Steyn. If you took those guys and you offered them to absolutely any side in the world right now, they’d bite your arm off.

BONGANI VO
The Proteas go into the competition as the 3rd ranked ODI side, and face stiff competition in their group, including previous World Cup winners India, Pakistan and the West Indies. So how do they fancy their chances this year?

FANIE DE VILLIERS
We’ve got the best chance ever.

AARON PHANGISO
We’ve got the team to go through and bring the trophy home.

GRAEME SMITH
Obviously – Proteas to win.

POMMIE MBANGWA
South Africa need this, that’s what I think.

AB DE VILLIERS
We’re going to win it.

BONGANI VO
And if they do, the fans will surely rejoice.

CHILDREN:
PROTEA FIRE!!

The players making their world cup debuts this year, like Aaron Phangiso, treasure that spirit. AARON PHANGISO This is my honest opinion – I feel that our team represents everyone. It doesn’t matter which race or culture. I think we’ve got it right. AB DE VILLIERS The team culture is probably our biggest strength. So many different and unique people in our team. We get that team to work together. That’s very powerful. BONGANI VO The philosophy of #ProteaFire – playing as role models with values and a purpose larger than just cricket – began with former Proteas captain Graeme Smith. BONGANI Tell me about the origins of #ProteaFire. GRAEME SMITH We’d always just seen the Protea as a flower. We found out it was the first flower to regenerate after a fire, so fire and resilience became key things in our value system. We found out that Proteus was the Greek god. Because he could see the future he had to tell the truth, so honesty and truth. And to see how that has grown from a value perspective and the respect for the different cultures and diversity we have has been incredible. BONGANI As ambassadors, what would you want young kids to learn from those values? GRAEME SMITH I think the most important thing is to have a dream. This opportunity to represent South Africa and play for the Proteas was something I wanted youngsters to still endeavor to do. BONGANI For kids like this – primary cricket enthusiasts – the Proteas are big role models. And it would appear the spirit of #ProteaFire is contagious. BONGANI What does #ProteaFire mean to you? Vox Pop: It means that it helps you with your cricket. Thinking that they’re behind me, it’s the fire, and then you play your heart out and do the best you can. Vox Pop: Everything they do is all together. Vox Pop: It makes me feel like I’m a Protea. One day I’ll be up on that stage hopefully. So that’s why I get fired up. Vox Pop: I like the way they bat and bowl. Vox Pop: It means everything to them. More and more kids are taking cricket. They’re very passionate. They’ve got a fire burning in their hearts to support the Proteas and the sport of cricket. Vox Pop: It inspires me to do my best and score runs and take wickets. BONGANI The players know how many children like this look up to them. FARHAAN BERHARDIEN Definitely. We are role models. I grew up on the Cape Flats. For me and my peers it’s quite a big thing. Being that shining light does play a big role in how we carry ourselves on and off the field. BONGANI VO Hopefully this year, that ProteaFire magic will produce more spectacular moments, as the cricket World Cup always has in the past. Like Jonty Rhodes’s flying run-out of Inzamam ul-Haq in 1992, or Lance Klusener blasting his way to Player of the Tournament in 1999. And then there’ve been the notorious mishaps – dropped bats and dropped catches that swung crucial games. And the rain has never been kind to the Proteas, most notoriously in 1992, in South Africa’s semi-final against England, when a convoluted method of adjusting targets in the event of a rain delay revised South Africa’s target of needing 22 runs from 13 balls to needing 22 runs from 1 ball. POMMIE MBANGWA Many a South African will see those pictures of Kepler Wessels and the rest of them standing there and walking out onto the field and shaking hands with the English guys. Absolutely nothing you can do. That’s probably the worst one in terms of being powerless, because it’s the rules that make it like that, and you’re gone. Thanks for coming. BONGANI VO But win or lose, the Proteas have always had enormous support from their fans. A major event at Melrose Arch gave their supporters a chance to show their passion for the Proteas just before they flew out to Australia. T20 Captain Faf du Plessis speaks for the whole squad about how much the fans back home inspire them. FAF DU PLESSIS It makes a huge difference. The Aussies, especially, when you play against them… they’re really tough fans. They really get behind their people. When you go there and you play against them, you know you’re playing against them. So the fans help you a lot with that. BONGANI Well I’d pay a lot of money to see you beat Australia. FAF DU PLESSIS I’ll pay that money as well. In the final, that’d be great. GRAEME SMITH When you take on Australia, once you land there, the media, the public, everyone turns against you for the 6 weeks that you’re there. BONGANI VO But having the world’s top 2 one-day batsmen and the world’s top fast bowler in our squad surely gives the fans higher hopes than ever before. POMMIE MBANGWA AB de Villiers, Hashim Amla and Dale Steyn. If you took those guys and you offered them to absolutely any side in the world right now, they’d bite your arm off. BONGANI VO The Proteas go into the competition as the 3rd ranked ODI side, and face stiff competition in their group, including previous World Cup winners India, Pakistan and the West Indies. So how do they fancy their chances this year? FANIE DE VILLIERS We’ve got the best chance ever. AARON PHANGISO We’ve got the team to go through and bring the trophy home. GRAEME SMITH Obviously – Proteas to win. POMMIE MBANGWA South Africa need this, that’s what I think. AB DE VILLIERS We’re going to win it. BONGANI VO And if they do, the fans will surely rejoice. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We spend some time with the Proteas ahead of their 2015 Cricket World Cup campaign, and see how they’re going to take the #ProteaFire spirit with them Down Under.
metadata.Summary: The Proteas have provided some of South African sport’s most iconic and celebrated moments. We will briefly recap some of the highlights from the last 6 Cricket World Cups. We will interview some current players, including AB de Villiers, about the spirit and culture of the ultimate “nice guy” team, and get them to share their hopes and expectations for the 2015 World Cup, and what they think their chances are of lifting cricket’s most coveted trophy for the first time.
metadata.Further information: The Proteas are not only cricketers. They see themselves as ambassadors for South Africa. When they play cricket, they are not only playing for themselves, but for a whole nation of supporters. Cricket South Africa’s launch of the #ProteaFire campaign is about getting the public to better identify with the players and understand the values that the team lives by – humility, resilience, courage, adaptability, unity and respect. It is the Proteas’ mission to inspire South Africans through their actions on and off the field. It is this culture that we will explore and focus the insert around. We will also speak to former players or captains, to reflect on how the game has changed, reminisce about their fondest memories from previous World Cups, and share their thoughts on the current Proteas squad – both as a team of cricketers, and South African ambassadors.
